items.title: datasette-llm 0.1a11
items.raw_text: Release: datasette-llm 0.1a11 datasette-llm is the intermediate plugin for Datasette that supports configuring LLMs for use with other Datasette plugins. This release adds support for OpenAI-compatible endpoints, so you can configure Datasette to use an LLM hosted anywhere that talks the OpenAI pseudo-standard web protocol. This means that if you're running local models with LM Studio or Ollama or llama.cpp (which just hit v1.0.0 ) you can run Datasette via uvx like this: wget https://datasette.io/content.db uvx --with datasette-agent datasette \ --root --secret 1 \ -s plugins.datasette-llm.default_model ' { "model": "lmstudio-qwen", "model_name": "qwen/qwen3.8-27b", "api_base": "http://localhost:1234/v1" } ' content.db And you'll get a local server running a Datasette Agent instance powered by your local model! Tags: uv , datasette-agent , llm , datasette , llms , ai , generative-ai

items.title: datasette-vega 0.7
items.raw_text: Release: datasette-vega 0.7 A new release of Datasette's longest untouched plugin, for rendering charts (using Vega-Lite ) against data in a table or custom query. The last release was in July 2018! I finally bumped it for compatibility with the latest Datasette alphas, plus some cosmetic tweaks to make it work better with Datasette Lite . (Datasette Lite just gained the ability to run JavaScript plugins like this! I'll write more about that soon.) Since it works with Datasette Lite, the live demo in the README now links to this demo on Datasette Lite . Tags: datasette , visualisation , datasette-lite

items.title: Johns Hopkins University: Sheridan Libraries Launches New Digital Collections Site
items.raw_text: From JHSL: Now available at the click of a mouse : rare maps of Maryland dating as far back as the sixteenth century, the oral history of the Hopkins surgeon who implanted the first automatic defibrillator, records associated with Chinese indentured laborers in Cuba from 1855 to 1895, and much more. Johns Hopkins Sheridan Libraries is pleased to announce the launch of a new online site that provides expanded access to digitized and born-digital materials from the university’s special collections and archives. Freely available to anyone, anywhere in the world, the site serves as a central destination for discovering and engaging with unique primary source materials that document the history of Johns Hopkins, Baltimore, and communities around the world. “Digital collections are a strategic way that we connect people with the rare and unique materials in our care,” said Elisabeth Long , Sheridan Dean of University Libraries, Archives, and Museums. “By making these collections openly available online, we are extending access to Johns Hopkins’ rich array of resources and providing researchers, students, and lifelong learners everywhere with new opportunities to engage with the historical record.” [Clip] The site currently includes more than 15,500 items from 18 collections, including photographs, newspapers, journals, maps, audio recordings, moving images, and archival materials. items.title: How the world’s fires changed while humanity hit pause
items.raw_text: Wildfires occur worldwide, and they can sometimes become serious threats to people's lives. A series of massive bushfires from 2019 to 2020 swept across southeastern Australia and destroyed thousands of homes. Recently, the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires spread widely across the city, resulting in massive damage to local communities. Many things can cause wildfires, but humans are the only factor that can also make preventative efforts. Measuring people's impact on fire is difficult because of the mix of human and natural influences. A team led by Jianghao Wang, a professor at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, recently published a study in Cell Reports Sustainability comparing the COVID-19 era with other years. Data from the 2020 lockdowns suggest that lower human activity at this time had the net effect of lowering average fire activity. Read full article Comments

SpaceX returned its Starship rocket on Saturday—but there's a catch
items.raw_text: STARBASE, Texas —The black and silver ship fell out of the sky, emerging from the cloud deck near the very end of its flight. Incongruously, the rocket flew horizontal until the last moment when three Raptor rocket engines ignited and it swooped into a vertical position. Slowly, gently, haltingly, the Starship upper stage eased its way toward the waiting tower where two arms extended outward, awaiting expectantly. The margins are so incredibly narrow. Two nubs on either side of the rocket, each protruding only about one foot, were the only purchase the rocket would have on the arms. Then, less than a minute after it came into view, the Starship upper stage was snagged by the launch tower, as snug as you like. And so it was all over. SpaceX, nearly a quarter of a century after its founding, had just taken a hugely significant step toward developing and optimizing a massive, rapidly reusable rocket. Read full article Comments

items.title: James Webb telescope finds ice older than the star it orbits
items.raw_text: Beta Pictoris is a young star, roughly 20 million years old, and located about 64 light-years away from Earth. It is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rubble where planets are still forming—astronomers have already found three. In a new Science study, a team led by Sarah Betti, an astronomer at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, used the James Webb Space Telescope to look for ice in this disk. Researchers found both water and carbon dioxide ice. The water ice is glassy rather than crystalline, and it is mixed with carbon dioxide in roughly the same proportions we see in comets of our own Solar System. This suggests ingredients necessary to form water-rich worlds might be common around young stars. The missing ice Beta Pictoris is one of the best studied stars in the sky. Its disk was among the first ever imaged, back in 1984, and we see it almost exactly edge-on, which makes it a natural laboratory for studying how planetary systems grow. It's what astronomers call a debris disk, where the dust is constantly replenished by collisions among comets and planetesimals, small bodies that are the building blocks of planets. items.title: Winemakers are learning that conservation can be good for business
items.raw_text: More than 500 vineyards are scattered across the slopes and valleys of South Africa’s Western Cape , one of the world’s most biologically diverse landscapes. The region produces about 90 percent of South Africa’s wine , but winemakers there are increasingly struggling with drought, excessive heat and erratic rainfall. Temperatures in the region have risen 1.5 to 2 times faster than the global average over the past five decades. And extreme storms have become more intense as climate variability increases. The late 2010s brought a significant challenge for winemakers, as three years of severe drought placed vineyards under intense stress and reduced grape production. As climate variability places increasing pressure on grape production, many wine producers are building on sustainability measures that have long been part of vineyard management. items.title: Megastoring Microsoft voorbij, bedrijf wacht enorme nasleep
items.raw_text: Microsoft heeft de wereldwijde storing die sinds afgelopen donderdag miljoenen gebruikers trof inmiddels opgelost. De technische problemen bij Microsoft 365 legden in meer dan zeventig landen essentiële digitale communicatie plat en troffen ook in Nederland tal van organisaties. Het bedrijf heeft inmiddels publiekelijk excuses aangeboden voor de verstoring. Met het technische herstel is de rekening echter nog niet vereffend: klanten moeten achterstanden wegwerken en zullen aanspraak maken op compensatie. Volgens Microsoft ontstonden de problemen door een technisch mankement tijdens een upgrade van de netwerkcapaciteit. Het concern benadrukt dat er geen sprake was van een cyberaanval of een incident veroorzaakt door ai. Door de storing waren diensten als Outlook, Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint en Copilot urenlang beperkt of helemaal niet beschikbaar. Het bedrijf verklaarde vanochtend dat alle diensten weer functioneren. Eerder bood Microsoft excuses aan klanten en partners aan. ‘Het spijt ons enorm dat deze storing onze klanten en partners heeft getroffen’, liet het concern weten. Rechtspraak en overheden zwaar geraakt De storing maakte opnieuw duidelijk hoe afhankelijk Nederlandse organisaties zijn geworden van Microsoft 365. Vooral de Rechtspraak kreeg te maken met problemen rond e-mailverkeer. Rechtbanken konden berichten niet of vertraagd ontvangen en versturen, waardoor burgers en advocaten werden geraakt. Telefonische bereikbaarheid bleef wel intact. Daarnaast meldden diver

items.title: The OpenAI board member who fired Sam Altman says we still can’t trust AI CEOs
items.raw_text: Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life. Helen is a well-known figure in the AI safety and policy community, though she is perhaps best known for having served on the board of OpenAI, when she was one of four board members who voted to fire Sam Altman . That incident, now sometimes referred to as “the blip,” ended with Sam coming back as CEO, Helen resigning, and a new board of directors. OpenAI has since restructured entirely . But it’s worth remembering what Helen and the board were supposed to do: OpenAI’s nonprofit board existed specifically to make sure the company didn’t betray its mission to build safe AI by prioritizing profit and growth over safety. When the board actually tried to pull the lever, that accountability mechanism broke, and here we are. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . Now, the question of AI safety is everywhere . This summer, AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic broke out of their testing environments and hacked real companies.
